note:
v1, THE SKELETON of SLOW ENOUGH TO COUNT (chirper-three; the song I wanted to make). THE IDEA: a chord is a rhythm too fast to count. Strike anything steadily and fast enough and you hear a note; twice as fast is the octave above. So the song has one rule that picks its rhythms and its notes at once: WHAT STRIKES EVERY p SIXTEENTHS PLAYS THE NOTE WHOSE PERIOD IS p. The tempo is in the key: at 122.7756 a pulse every three sixteenths is F3 exactly six octaves down. Then, with nothing else chosen, common time itself is a C (the beat, the backbeat and the bar are C in three octaves), the dotted values are F (the djent chug), and the fives are A flat. Threes against the kit's four are the power chord; add the fives and the groove is F minor; the three come round together every 60 sixteenths and with the bar line every fifteen bars. Where threes and fives meet is the note they are both harmonics of, D flat. Every third three is a nine: B flat.
THE FORM IS THE PROOF, BOTH WAYS. 0:00 three toms, tuned F3, C3 and A flat 2 (the album kit's own tuning), each rolled at its own note (174.6, 131.0 and 104.8 strokes a second): you hear a chord. 0:02 the three rolls slow down together, an octave a bar for six bars. 0:13.7 they arrive in tempo as threes, fours and fives: the chord is still in the heads, and its speed is now a rhythm. At each meeting a pulse goes to the band: 0:21.0 F (kick, bass, two guitars), 0:28.3 A flat (two more guitars), 0:35.7 C, which is the cymbal and the snare: common time. 0:43 MINOR, the whole chord for one cycle of fifteen bars. 1:12.3 SIXTH: the low D flat sounds wherever threes and fives meet, a bar less a sixteenth apart, so the band's biggest stroke comes a sixteenth earlier every bar and is home after fifteen. 1:41.6 FOURTH, the quiet middle: B flat every nine on the left, D flat every fifteen on the right, no guitars chugging, the F pulse on the foot alone, the hands on the closed hat. 2:11.0 COMMON: everyone on C, in sixteenths, eighths, quarters and the bar; by the rule the plainest thing a band can play is the dominant. 2:26.6 HOME: F minor, everything; the toms rejoin at 2:48.6. 2:55.9 the three toms alone speed up, an octave a bar, until the rhythm is the chord again; 3:07.7 the band plays that chord. 100 bars, 3:15 of music.
WHAT IS IN IT: the album's own rigs and kit under their own names (ct-twin on two amps, the wall pair, ct-bass, ct-kit); nothing new and no library patch touched. Every voice is one note at one rate, with an accent on every second and fourth stroke (its octaves below). No fills, no lead, no words.
WHAT I MEASURED (finished files, seeds 0 and 11; I cannot listen). The held chord's three strongest lines are A flat 2, C3 and F3: 104.7, 130.9 and 176.0 Hz (0, -0.8, -4.8 dB) on seed 0 and 104.7, 131.1 and 174.3 Hz (0, -1.8, -7.2 dB) on seed 11; the F is the weakest of the three on both. At the end, while the roll still holds under the band's chord, the same three lead on seed 0 (130.7, 104.7, 175.6 Hz, the bass's F at 43.8); on seed 11 the A flat and the F are 7 and 13 dB under the C. AFTER THE ROLL STOPS the band's own chord is led by C3 and the low F (130.9, 43.6, 87.3 Hz) and its A flat is not among the six strongest lines: the guitars' minor third is weak against the power chord under it. Strokes lose 3 dB for each octave of speed; with that for all three drums the roll stayed within 1.1 dB (raw, K) from the held chord to the counted strokes. The F tom's line was then 9.5 dB under the other two, so it loses 2.2 dB an octave; the 1.1 dB was not taken again after that. Level by section (K, dB, both seeds within 0.3): held -14.5, unwound -15.8, toms in tempo -17.0, then -13.1, -12.7, -12.2 as the three pulses enter; minor -12.0, sixth -11.4, fourth -13.7, common -10.9, home -11.3, wound -15.8, the chord -10.9. FIRST TWO TAKES, not kept: with the toms at the kit's usual fader the three drums alone were as loud as the whole band (-12.0 against -12.4, measured on the second) and the scorer read 1.7 and 2.0 dB between the loudest and quietest sections; they scored 94.6 and 94.8. The second already had the fourth without its guitars; the kept take also has the toms 5.5 dB down.
SCORES 0/11: 97.171/97.370. The weak term is variety (85.6/86.6: the scorer reads 3.8 dB between its loudest and quietest sections); every other term is 98.9 or over. -10.0 LUFS, -1.29 dBTP.
WHICH OF HARRY'S RULES I TOOK AS BINDING on a song he said to go crazy on: the steady pulse and the long cycle that lines up, no number in the title, the record's guitars and kit, new names only. What I took as mine: there is no riff, only pulses, and the harmony is whatever the rule gives (F minor, D flat, B flat minor, C), not the record's hook.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether the opening reads as a chord coming apart or as thirteen seconds of drum machine; whether a groove made only of steady pulses holds for fifteen bars at a time; whether the D flat sliding earlier is felt as one long gesture or as a band coming in wrong.

next: It is anyone's now. What the skeleton lacks, roughly in the order I would do it: (1) TUNE IT (an instrument round), and with it the last chord's A flat, which the guitars barely sound (see the note): the pulses are pure and the guitars are not: the fives are a minor third 16 cents wider than the guitars' A flat, the D flat is 14 cents wide, and the A flat tom sits 16 cents under its own roll. A song-local tuning for the guitars and the kit's tom pitches would make the band's last chord and the wound-up chord the same notes. (2) THE TWO PULSES NOT USED: every 7 is a D a third of a semitone sharp and every 11 a G flat a quarter-tone sharp (track 1's other wheels); a clean guitar or a lead on them wants that tuning first. (3) A TUNE under the same rule: a line in which every note lasts as long as its pitch says (F 3, 6 or 12 sixteenths, C 4 or 8, A flat 5 or 10, B flat 9, D flat 15), so it speeds up as it climbs. (4) the drummer: fills at the meetings, and something for the hands in 'common'. (5) dynamics: 'fourth' is only 2 dB under 'minor'. (6) a choice for an ear: whether the band should strike its chord once at 0:00 so the buzz is known for what it is. THE KNOBS: C10T14_ROLL is 'velocity ; dB a stroke loses per octave of speed ; the same for the F tom ; bars the chord is held at each end'; C10T14_TOMS is the toms' fader (-1.5dB). Do not break the rule to add interest: a voice may change its rate, and then it changes its note.

note: chirp-eco, a measurement for whoever draws this next, not a judgment (tools/sendpaths.py on v1): the snare and the toms sit on the drums bus, which has a clip, and are also sent to the overheads bus (oh) at -1.5 dB, which does not pass through it: a path round the clip, the same shape Common Time's snare had from v10 to v40 (there its peak was 6.3 dB higher with the send and half its loudness came through the room; the ear later said the path was part of the sound in one song and a fault in two). The cymbals and hat at +4.5 dB to oh are the room they live in. `python3 tools/sendpaths.py chirpers10-t14 --measure FROM-TO` gives the numbers for this song; whether it is a fault is for the ear.
